items.title: Safe AWS setup
items.body:
STEP 1 — Sign up.
  Open the AWS signup card. Use a real email + real card. Pick 'Basic Support — Free'.

STEP 2 — Turn on MFA (multi-factor auth) on the root user.
  In AWS console, click your name (top right) → Security credentials → MFA → Add.
  Use an authenticator app (Google Authenticator or Authy).

STEP 3 — Set a billing alarm at $5.
  In console search bar, type 'CloudWatch' → Alarms → Create alarm → Billing → Total Estimated Charge → set threshold $5 → notify your email.
  Now if your bill ever hits $5 you get an email.

STEP 4 — Create an IAM user for daily use (NEVER use root again).
  In console search bar: 'IAM' → Users → Create user.
  Username: forge-dev. Attach policy: AdministratorAccess.
  After creating, click the user → Security credentials → Create access key → 'Command line interface' → save the Access Key ID + Secret Access Key in a password manager.

STEP 5 — Install AWS CLI.
  Mac: brew install awscli
  Win: download from https://aws.amazon.com/cli/
  Linux: sudo apt install awscli
  Then: aws configure
  Paste your Access Key + Secret. Region: us-east-1. Output: json.

STEP 6 — Verify.
      aws sts get-caller-identity
  YOU SHOULD SEE: your IAM user ARN (not root).

items.title: Terraform download (official)

items.title: First Terraform resource
items.body:
STEP 1 — Install Terraform.
  Mac: brew install terraform
  Win: download zip, unzip, add to PATH (or use Chocolatey)
  Linux: follow the official Linux instructions
  Verify: terraform version → should print 1.x.x.

STEP 2 — Make an infra folder.
      cd Desktop/edge-portfolio
      mkdir infra
      cd infra

STEP 3 — Write your first main.tf.
  In VS Code, new file: edge-portfolio/infra/main.tf. Type:

      terraform {
        required_providers {
          aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" }
        }
      }
      provider "aws" {
        region = "us-east-1"
      }
      resource "aws_s3_bucket" "portfolio" {
        bucket = "YOUR-NAME-edge-portfolio-2026"
      }

  Replace YOUR-NAME with your real name (lowercase, no spaces). S3 bucket names are GLOBALLY unique — yours must not exist anywhere.

STEP 4 — Run Terraform.
      terraform init
  YOU SHOULD SEE: 'Terraform has been successfully initialized!'
      terraform plan
  YOU SHOULD SEE: 'Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.'
      terraform apply
  Type 'yes' when asked.
  YOU SHOULD SEE: 'Apply complete! Resources: 1 added'

STEP 5 — Verify in AWS.
  In the AWS console, search 'S3'. You see your bucket. Your first cloud resource.

items.title: Push the IaC
items.body:
STEP 1 — Make a .gitignore in edge-portfolio/.
  New file: .gitignore. Type:
      .terraform/
      *.tfstate
      *.tfstate.backup
      .terraform.lock.hcl

      # Edge Portfolio
      My personal portfolio, deployed on AWS S3 + CloudFront, provisioned with Terraform.
      
      ## Live URL
      https://xxxxxxxx.cloudfront.net  (paste yours)
      
      ## Cost
      < $1 / month at free-tier S3 + CloudFront usage.
      
      ## How to deploy (someone forking this repo)
      1. Install AWS CLI + Terraform.
      2. Configure AWS: aws configure
      3. Edit infra/main.tf — change the bucket name to something unique.
      4. cd infra && terraform init && terraform apply

      6. Wait 5 min for CloudFront. Visit the URL from terraform output.

STEP 3 — Push.
  Open the 'create new repository' card. Name: edge-portfolio. Public. Create.
  In your terminal:
      cd Desktop/edge-portfolio
      git init
      git add .
      git commit -m "Edge Portfolio v0.1 — IaC for S3 + CloudFront"
      git branch -M main
      git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/edge-portfolio.git
      git push -u origin main

days.title: Test the destroy + redeploy
days.summary: Today you test what real engineers test: can you wipe and rebuild from scratch?

items.title: Destroy and redeploy
items.body:
STEP 1 — Take down everything.
      cd Desktop/edge-portfolio/infra
      terraform destroy
  Type 'yes'. All AWS resources are deleted.

STEP 2 — Verify the site is GONE.
  Visit your CloudFront URL — it should now error.

STEP 3 — Rebuild from scratch.
      terraform apply
  Type 'yes'. Wait 10 minutes for CloudFront.
  Re-upload index.html: aws s3 cp ../index.html s3://YOUR-BUCKET/

STEP 4 — Site is BACK.
  Open the new CloudFront URL (it changed!). Update your README with the new URL.
  Push the README update:
      git add README.md && git commit -m "Update CloudFront URL after redeploy" && git push

PASS CRITERIA — Edge Portfolio v0.1 ships when:
  ☐ main.tf creates S3 + CloudFront + OAI + bucket policy
  ☐ Live CloudFront URL serves your portfolio over HTTPS
  ☐ terraform destroy + terraform apply works clean (reproducible)
  ☐ Public GitHub repo named edge-portfolio
  ☐ README has the live URL + how-to-fork instructions
  ☐ .gitignore excludes .terraform/ and *.tfstate

weeks.title: Edge Portfolio v0.3: GitHub Actions CI/CD
weeks.context: Right now you manually upload index.html. This week you automate it — push to main, the site auto-deploys.

items.title: Pipeline plan
items.body:
What should the pipeline do on every push to main?
  1. Run html-validator (catch broken HTML)
  2. Sync the file to S3
  3. Invalidate CloudFront cache

items.title: Least-privilege CI user
items.body:
In AWS Console → IAM → Users → Create user → name: github-actions-ci
Don't give AdminAccess. Create a custom policy with ONLY:
  s3:PutObject, s3:DeleteObject on your portfolio bucket
  cloudfront:CreateInvalidation on your distribution

Save the Access Key ID + Secret.

items.title: Repository secrets
items.body:
In GitHub → your repo → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret.
Add:
  AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID = (the new CI user key)
  AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = (the secret)
  AWS_S3_BUCKET = your bucket name
  AWS_CLOUDFRONT_ID = your CloudFront distribution ID

items.title: .github/workflows/deploy.yml
items.body:
Create .github/workflows/deploy.yml:

      name: Deploy
      on:
        push:
          branches: [main]
          paths: ['index.html']
      jobs:
        deploy:
          runs-on: ubuntu-latest
          steps:
            - uses: actions/checkout@v4
            - name: Configure AWS credentials
              uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
              with:
                aws-access-key-id: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
                aws-secret-access-key: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
                aws-region: us-east-1
            - name: Sync to S3
              run: aws s3 cp index.html s3://${{ secrets.AWS_S3_BUCKET }}/
            - name: Invalidate CloudFront
              run: aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id ${{ secrets.AWS_CLOUDFRONT_ID }} --paths '/index.html' '/'

items.title: Push a change
items.body:
Make a small edit to index.html (e.g. update your tagline). Commit + push to main.
Go to GitHub → your repo → Actions tab. Watch the workflow run.
After ~1 min, refresh your live site — the change should be live.

items.title: Quality gate
items.body:
Before the S3 sync step, add:
            - name: Validate HTML
              uses: Cyb3r-Jak3/html5validator-action@v7
              with:
                root: '.'

Now if you write broken HTML, the workflow fails BEFORE deploying.

topics: Metrics vs logs vs traces — the three pillars
Prometheus — pull-based metrics, PromQL fundamentals
Grafana — dashboards, alerting, data source connections
Loki — Prometheus-style logs (label-based, no full-text)
Tempo — distributed tracing storage
OpenTelemetry — the open standard for instrumentation
USE method (Brendan Gregg) — Utilisation, Saturation, Errors
RED method (Tom Wilkie) — Rate, Errors, Duration

weeks.project: Add Full Observability to Your K8s App. Install Prometheus + Grafana + Loki + Tempo. Instrument your app with OpenTelemetry. Build a Grafana dashboard with: RED metrics, resource usage, error rate, deploy markers. Set up 5 alerts: high error rate, high latency, low success rate, pod crash, disk space. Document in OBSERVABILITY.md.

weeks.title: SRE — SLOs, Error Budgets, On-Call
weeks.context: SRE is the discipline of operating software at scale. The core ideas: SLOs (service level objectives), error budgets (you're allowed to fail this much), and on-call (with proper rotation, escalation, post-mortems). This week you adopt them.
topics: SLIs, SLOs, SLAs — definitions, common confusions
Error budgets — how they enable velocity
Burn-rate alerts — multi-window, multi-burn-rate
Toil — what it is, how to track and eliminate it
Blameless post-mortems — the structure, why blame is counterproductive
On-call rotations — sustainability, paging policies
Runbooks — when an alert fires, what do you do?
Capacity planning — predicting when you'll need more resources
tasks: Define 3 SLIs for your URL shortener: availability, latency, success rate
Define corresponding SLOs (e.g. 99.5% availability, p95 < 500ms)
Configure burn-rate alerts based on those SLOs
Write a runbook for one alert: 'high error rate'; document the diagnosis + fix steps
Conduct a mock post-mortem for a real incident (or simulated outage) using the template
weeks.project: Define and Implement SLOs for Your URL Shortener. Pick realistic SLOs (don't go 99.99%). Configure burn-rate alerts in Prometheus/Grafana. Write runbooks for the top 5 alert types. Set up PagerDuty (or BetterStack) for on-call paging. Document everything in SLOS.md + RUNBOOKS.md. Simulate one incident and run a post-mortem.

weeks.title: Cost Optimisation — FinOps and the AWS Bill
weeks.context: Cloud bills surprise everyone. FinOps — the discipline of cloud cost management — is now a real specialisation. This week you tag everything, build cost dashboards, and apply the patterns that cut bills by 30-50%.
topics: AWS Cost Explorer + budgets — built-in tools
Tagging strategy — every resource gets cost-attribution tags
Right-sizing — instances that are 5% utilised
Spot instances — the 70-90% discount on interruption-tolerant workloads
Savings plans + reserved instances — committing to save
S3 storage classes — IA, Glacier, deletion lifecycle
Egress fees — why the same data costs differently per cloud
Tools — Vantage, CloudHealth, Kubecost for K8s
tasks: Audit your AWS bill via Cost Explorer; identify the top 5 line items
Tag all your resources with `environment`, `project`, `owner`
Right-size one over-provisioned EC2 / EBS volume
Move an interruption-tolerant workload to Spot instances
Install Kubecost on your K8s cluster; observe per-pod cost
weeks.project: Cut Your AWS Bill by 30%. Apply: right-sizing, Spot for non-prod, S3 lifecycle policies (IA after 30d, Glacier after 90d), Reserved Instances or Savings Plans for steady workloads. Document the journey in FINOPS.md with before/after numbers. Set up a monthly review process.

weeks.title: Disaster Recovery — Backups, Multi-Region, and Tested Restores
weeks.context: Untested backups don't exist. This week you set up proper backups, multi-region replication, and — critically — you actually restore from backup, end-to-end. Most teams discover their backups are broken only during a real disaster.
topics: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) vs RPO (Recovery Point Objective)
Backup strategies — full, incremental, differential
Database backups — pg_dump vs WAL archiving, point-in-time recovery
Cross-region replication — S3 CRR, RDS read replicas across regions
Application-level backup tools — Velero for K8s
Tested restores — quarterly fire drills
Disaster scenarios — region outage, accidental delete, ransomware
Runbook for region failover
tasks: Enable automated daily backups on your RDS instance
Configure point-in-time recovery; restore to a 6-hour-ago state in a test environment
Enable S3 cross-region replication for one bucket
Install Velero on your K8s cluster; back up + restore a namespace
Write a disaster recovery runbook for one realistic scenario (RDS region down)
weeks.project: Build a Tested Disaster Recovery Plan. For your URL shortener: automated daily backups (RDS, S3), 30-day retention, point-in-time recovery, cross-region S3 replication for static assets, Velero for K8s state. Perform a full restore drill: spin up a new region from backups, verify functionality. Document in DR.md.

weeks.title: Cloud Security Posture — IAM, Network, Audit
weeks.context: Cloud breaches happen via misconfigured IAM (the most common), public S3 buckets (the second most common), and unauthorised access (the third). This week you scan your cloud for vulnerabilities and fix them.

Network segmentation — public vs private subnets, security groups, NACLs
CloudTrail + AWS Config — auditing what happened
GuardDuty + Security Hub — threat detection
Open-source scanners — Prowler, ScoutSuite, Cloudsplaining
Compliance frameworks — SOC2, ISO27001 as engineering targets
Incident response — when your cloud is breached
tasks: Enable CloudTrail, AWS Config, GuardDuty in your AWS account
Run Prowler against your AWS account; document every finding above LOW
